reason: The text explicitly depicts collaboration between leaders and people throughout. All Israel gathers to David at Hebron (v. 1), recognizing him as their leader ('bone and flesh'). The elders of Israel formally covenant with David (v. 3), establishing mutual agreement. The passage repeatedly emphasizes unified action: 'David and all Israel' go to Jerusalem together (v. 4), the mighty men are described as 'strengthening themselves with him in his kingdom, with all Israel' (v. 3, beginning of mighty men section). The military accounts demonstrate collaborative effort—warriors such as the three mighty men break through the Philistine camp together and present water to David (v. 18-19), and Benaiah and other warriors perform deeds 'with' David (עִמּוֹ). The covenant-making itself is a formal expression of reciprocal commitment between leader and people.
